books.section: Topic 4.3 Politics and Regional Interests, C. A Temporary Truce on the Slavery Question in the Pre-Civil War Period

stimulus.text: Paraphrase of the House of Representatives’ gag rule, first adopted in 1836: Any petition or resolution about slavery would be laid on the table without being read, printed, or debated. The rule stayed in force until 1844. Former president John Quincy Adams, then a member of the House from Massachusetts, fought the rule in every session.
stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of the House gag resolutions (Pinckney resolutions), 1836-1844, as described in Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.3 C, and Princeton Review 25e, Chapter 8, 'The Abolition Movement.'

source: original; stimulus paraphrases the House gag rule, 1836-1844, from the grounding books
stem: Southern members of the House pushed for the gag rule mainly because

options.text: they wanted to keep slavery off the floor of Congress
they wanted more debate about abolition in the House
options.misconception: More debate is the opposite of a gag; the rule ended debate by tabling every petition.

options.text: they hoped to pass a law ending slavery
options.misconception: Southern members defended slavery; ending it was the abolitionists’ goal, not theirs.

options.text: they wanted the Supreme Court to decide the question
options.misconception: The rule was about House debate, not about sending the question to the Court.

rationales.A: Abolitionists were flooding the House with petitions, and every one forced slavery onto the floor. The gag rule tabled them all, so the subject never came up.
rationales.B: A gag rule silences debate; it does not invite more of it. Southern members wanted the subject gone, not discussed.
rationales.C: Southern members pushed the rule to protect slavery, not to end it. The law they wanted was silence, not emancipation.
rationales.D: The rule says nothing about the Court. It is a House procedure for House business, aimed at House debate.
rationales.general:
1. Ask what abolitionists were doing. Sending antislavery petitions to the House in large numbers.
2. Ask what each petition did. It put slavery on the floor for debate.
3. Ask what the rule did. It tabled every petition unread, so slavery never reached the floor.
4. Put it together. The rule’s purpose was to keep the subject out of Congress.
Background: beginning in the 1830s, abolitionists pressed congressmen to introduce antislavery resolutions, and Southern politicians answered with resolutions to table them automatically.
Remember: to find a rule’s purpose, ask what problem it makes go away.
